title: Abstract
text:
Abstract




High landscape connectivity supports the conservation of large mammals, but for wild boar (Sus scrofa) it also promotes the geographic spread of African Swine Fever (ASF), a viral disease with a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent and no available vaccine. As ASF expands westward across Europe, wildlife and veterinary authorities in Switzerland need spatially explicit tools that show how landscape interventions such as fences or wildlife crossings would change wild boar movement and disease spread risk. Existing connectivity models for the Swiss Mittelland are rigorous but static, and they cannot answer interactive scenario questions.
This thesis develops a species-specific resistance surface for wild boar and an interactive QGIS plugin that lets users test landscape modifications without programming knowledge. The resistance surface was calibrated empirically from GPS telemetry of 36 wild boar tracked in Canton Aargau between 2014 and 2017. Directed transit movements were separated from resting behaviour with a rule-based classifier, and an integrated step-selection function estimated habitat preferences from 7,810 transit steps. The selection coefficients were converted into a 25-metre resistance raster using the Keeley exponential transformation, and the calibrated model was transferred to Canton Zürich without re-estimation. The plugin combines five complementary analyses on the resulting surface: least-cost path corridors, circuit-theory pinch points, a cost-distance infection-risk kernel anchored to the EFSA operational zones, a biased correlated random walk, and an iSSF-based individual movement model of disease spread.
Seven landscape covariates were significant positive predictors of transit movement, with forest density at the local scale and distance to railway showing the strongest effects. The resulting resistance surfaces reproduce the known corridor structure of both cantons, concentrating low resistance along forested slopes and riparian zones. The plugin runs all five analyses in under three minutes and reacts correctly to user-placed fences and crossings, redistributing modelled corridors and contracting infection-risk zones in response. The tool is best understood as a pre-outbreak planning instrument that helps authorities identify priority fence locations before an ASF incursion occurs. Its main limitation is the absence of independent validation in the Zürich transfer area, which remains the most important next step.

Zusammenfassung
Eine hohe Landschaftskonnektivität unterstützt den Schutz grosser Säugetiere, fördert beim Wildschwein (Sus scrofa) jedoch zugleich die geografische Ausbreitung der Afrikanischen Schweinepest (ASP), einer Viruserkrankung mit einer Letalität von 90 bis 95 Prozent und ohne verfügbaren Impfstoff. Da sich die ASP in Europa weiter nach Westen ausbreitet, benötigen Wildhut und Veterinärbehörden in der Schweiz räumlich explizite Werkzeuge, die zeigen, wie sich bauliche Eingriffe wie Zäune oder Wildtierüberführungen auf die Bewegung von Wildschweinen und das Ausbreitungsrisiko auswirken. Die bestehenden Konnektivitätsmodelle für das Schweizer Mittelland sind methodisch fundiert, aber statisch und erlauben keine interaktive Szenarienanalyse.
Diese Arbeit entwickelt eine artspezifische Widerstandsoberfläche für das Wildschwein sowie ein interaktives QGIS-Plugin, mit dem Anwenderinnen und Anwender ohne Programmierkenntnisse Landschaftsveränderungen testen können. Die Widerstandsoberfläche wurde empirisch aus GPS-Telemetriedaten von 36 Wildschweinen kalibriert, die zwischen 2014 und 2017 im Kanton Aargau besendert wurden. Gerichtete Wanderbewegungen wurden mit einem regelbasierten Klassifikator vom Ruheverhalten getrennt, und eine integrierte Step-Selection-Funktion schätzte die Habitatpräferenzen aus 7810 Transitschritten. Die Selektionskoeffizienten wurden mit der exponentiellen Keeley-Transformation in ein 25-Meter-Widerstandsraster überführt, und das kalibrierte Modell wurde ohne Neuschätzung auf den Kanton Zürich übertragen. Das Plugin verbindet fünf sich ergänzende Analysen: Least-Cost-Path-Korridore, Engstellen aus der Schaltkreistheorie, einen distanzbasierten Infektionsrisiko-Kernel entlang der EFSA-Zonen, einen biased correlated random walk sowie ein iSSF-basiertes individuenbasiertes Ausbreitungsmodell.
Sieben Landschaftsvariablen waren signifikante positive Prädiktoren der Transitbewegung, wobei die lokale Walddichte und die Distanz zur Bahnlinie die stärksten Effekte zeigten. Die resultierenden Widerstandsoberflächen geben die bekannte Korridorstruktur beider Kantone wieder und konzentrieren geringe Widerstände entlang bewaldeter Hänge und Gewässerräume. Das Plugin führt alle fünf Analysen in weniger als drei Minuten aus und reagiert korrekt auf von Nutzenden platzierte Zäune und Überführungen, indem es die modellierten Korridore umverteilt und die Risikozonen verkleinert. Das Werkzeug eignet sich vor allem als Planungsinstrument vor einem Ausbruch und hilft den Behörden, prioritäre Zaunstandorte frühzeitig zu bestimmen. Die wichtigste Einschränkung ist die fehlende unabhängige Validierung im Übertragungsgebiet Zürich, die den zentralen nächsten Schritt darstellt.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Problem Statement
The Swiss Mittelland is among the most densely settled and intensively managed landscapes in Central Europe. Roads, railways, urban expansion and intensive agriculture collectively form a network of barriers that fragments natural habitats and restricts the free movement of wildlife across the region. For large mammals, this fragmentation carries serious long-term consequences: reduced population exchange, diminishing genetic diversity and, ultimately, a decline in regional population viability (Fischer et al. 2024; Urbina et al. 2023). In a landscape as structurally altered as the Canton of Zurich, restoring meaningful ecological connectivity is therefore an active and ongoing challenge for wildlife managers and spatial planners.
In response, spatial planning frequently relies on targeted structural interventions such as wildlife overpasses and underpasses, whose effectiveness for species like red deer (Cervus elaphus) has been documented across Switzerland and neighbouring France (Fischer et al. 2024; Urbina et al. 2023). Assessing where such infrastructure is most needed requires spatially explicit connectivity models. Robust frameworks for this purpose have been established and validated at the regional scale by Urbina et al. (2023) and, more recently, for the Swiss Mittelland by Fischer et al. (2024), producing maps of movement corridors, pinch points and connectivity bottlenecks that can directly guide conservation planning.
What these models have not yet addressed is a parallel management challenge. Unlike red deer, the wild boar (Sus scrofa) is not primarily a species in need of connectivity enhancement. It is the primary wildlife reservoir of African Swine Fever (ASF), a viral disease with a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent in infected animals for which no effective vaccine exists (Guberti et al. 2019). High landscape connectivity for wild boar directly facilitates the geographic spread of ASF, meaning that interventions designed to benefit species like red deer can simultaneously increase disease transmission risk for wild boar across the same landscape.
This conflict between promoting connectivity for conservation and restricting it to prevent disease spread is not new to ecological theory. Hess (1994) demonstrated formally that conservation corridors can, under certain epidemiological conditions, dramatically increase the risk of disease-driven population extinction. The epidemiology of ASF in wild boar matches those conditions closely enough to make this trade-off a concrete management problem for wildlife authorities, particularly as ASF continues to expand its range westward across Europe.
The connectivity models developed by Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023) are methodologically rigorous and well validated, but they are static representations of the current landscape. They do not allow practitioners to test hypothetical scenarios interactively. A wildlife manager or veterinary authority asking what would happen to ASF spread risk if a fence were installed along a specific road, or what connectivity a proposed wildlife overpass would deliver for red deer, currently has no tool to answer that question dynamically. This gap between analytical capability and operational decision support is the direct motivation for this thesis.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Objectives
This thesis develops an interactive spatial planning tool in the form of a QGIS plugin that models functional connectivity for wild boar across the Canton of Zurich. The plugin allows users to dynamically alter the underlying landscape resistance surface by placing hypothetical infrastructure elements, such as movement barriers or wildlife crossings, directly on the map. After each modification, the model recalculates the resulting connectivity and visualises the effect on potential ASF spread corridors and pinch points. The underlying methodology adapts the resistance surface construction, least-cost path calculation and circuit-theory-based corridor modeling approach of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023), with all parameters specifically tailored to the ecology and movement behaviour of wild boar.
Two specific objectives guide this work. The first is the methodological adaptation of the existing connectivity modeling framework for wild boar, including the classification of wild boar telemetry data into in-matrix and in-patch movement, the fitting of an integrated Step Selection Function based on spatial covariantes and finally the construction of a species-specific resistance surface. The second is the development of an interactive QGIS plugin that allows end users to simulate ASF spread from a specific location with different connectivity models and structural landscape changes without requiring programming knowledge.

title: 2  Theoretical Background
text:
2.1 Ecological Connectivity in Fragmented Landscapes
This chapter sets out the concepts the thesis relies on: landscape connectivity and its modeling, the movement ecology of the wild boar, and the epidemiology of African Swine Fever (ASF), which together make connectivity a key factor in disease management.
Landscape connectivity describes the degree to which a landscape facilitates or impedes the movement of organisms among habitat patches. Taylor et al. (1993) formalised the concept as a vital structural element of landscapes, and it is now standard to separate two dimensions. Structural connectivity refers to the physical arrangement of habitat in space and can be read from land cover maps alone. Functional connectivity reflects the behavioural response of a specific species to that structure (Urbina et al. 2023; Tischendorf et al. 2003), so two structurally identical landscapes can differ greatly depending on whether the target species treats roads, rivers, or fields as permeable or as barriers. A resistance surface calibrated for one species therefore cannot simply be reused for another. This distinction matters in the Swiss Mittelland, which looks connected on a coarse map but is functionally fragmented for large mammals by dense road and rail networks, urban development, and intensive agriculture, leading to reduced gene flow and limited recolonisation for species such as red deer and wild boar (Fischer et al. 2024; Urbina et al. 2023).

title: 2  Theoretical Background
text:
2.2 Modeling Functional Connectivity
The following section provides a theoretical explanation of all the modeling methods for functional connectivity used in this study.

2.2.1 Resistance Surfaces and the Integrated Step-Selection Function
The resistance surface is the core spatial input to all functional connectivity models. It is a raster in which each cell carries a value representing the relative cost of movement, with high-quality habitat assigned low resistance and barriers such as motorways assigned very high or infinite resistance. Resistance can be assigned from expert judgement or, more defensibly, estimated empirically from GPS tracking. Urbina et al. (2023) derived resistance for red deer from over 85,000 GPS fixes of 15 individuals across the Greater Geneva agglomeration at 5-metre resolution, and Fischer et al. (2024) applied a comparable empirical framework to the Swiss Mittelland. Finer resolution resolves the narrow infrastructure that constrains large-mammal movement but multiplies the cell count and the computational cost.
Where GPS data are available, the integrated step-selection function (iSSF) provides a principled basis for this estimation (Avgar et al. 2016). The iSSF reconstructs movement as a sequence of steps, each with a step length and turning angle, and compares every observed step against random alternatives drawn from the same movement kernel. Fitting a conditional logistic regression of the form \(w(x) = \exp\!\left(\sum_k \hat{\beta}_k x_k\right)\) yields selection coefficients \(\hat{\beta}_k\) that express habitat preference while holding movement capacity and availability constant. This separates genuine preference from mere abundance: an animal seen often in forest may prefer forest, or forest may simply be plentiful where it started, and the conditional design distinguishes the two. To turn the coefficients into resistance on the scale required by corridor models, Keeley et al. (2016) proposed the transformation \(R = \exp\!\left(-c \cdot \hat{\beta}_k x_k\right)\), where the sign is reversed so that strongly selected cells receive low resistance. A single tracking dataset therefore yields a resistance surface that is both species-specific and statistically grounded.








Figure 2.1: Schematic of the integrated step-selection function and the resulting resistance surface. Left: at each observed location the animal’s realised step (solid arrow) is compared against random available steps (dashed arrows) drawn from its movement kernel, so the model learns which features are selected. Right: the fitted coefficients are translated into a resistance raster, where preferred habitat receives low resistance (green) and barriers such as roads receive high resistance (red).







2.2.2 Least-Cost Paths and Circuit Theory
Least-cost path (LCP) analysis was among the first methods to use resistance surfaces for corridor mapping (Adriaensen et al. 2003). It identifies the single route between two patches that minimises cumulative resistance. It is computationally cheap and widely used, but it assumes movement along one optimal route and says nothing about whether alternative routes exist or how redundant the surrounding landscape is (McRae et al. 2008).
Circuit theory addresses that limitation by treating the resistance surface as an electrical network in which current flows from a source to a ground through all available pathways at once (McRae et al. 2008). McRae et al. (2008) showed that the current through any cell is proportional to the expected number of times a random walker would pass through it, giving the method a process-based interpretation that LCP lacks. High current density marks heavily used corridors, and points where the landscape forces nearly all movement through a single passage are called pinch points, which are the highest-priority targets for intervention because losing a small area there disproportionately reduces connectivity. Because effective resistance falls as parallel routes are added, the method also captures redundancy, and the ratio of least-cost to resistance distance measures how much a single bottleneck dominates. The Circuitscape software solves networks of millions of cells, making it applicable at landscape scale. Urbina et al. (2023) applied Circuitscape 5 to a graph of 172 core areas and 424 links in Greater Geneva, mapping the major corridors and confirming the role of specific wildlife overpasses.








Figure 2.2: Schematic contrast between least-cost path and circuit theory on the same landscape, with a source (S), a target (T), and a barrier that has a single gap. Left: least-cost path analysis returns only the single cheapest route. Right: circuit theory spreads movement across all parallel routes at once, and where the landscape forces flow through the narrow gap a pinch point forms (arrow), which least-cost analysis cannot reveal.







2.2.3 Infection-Risk Kernels and Cost-Distance Dispersal
An infection-risk kernel converts a cost-distance analysis into the probability that a dispersing infected animal reaches a given location before dying. Dispersal is described by an exponential kernel \(P(d) = \exp(-d/D)\), where \(d\) is a distance measure and \(D\) is a characteristic dispersal scale set from telemetry. The single parameter \(D\) has a direct probabilistic interpretation and can be read from the literature. For wild boar, the relevant scale during the infectious period is the mean natal dispersal distance rather than the home-range diameter, because infected animals move normally until the final clinical phase. Telemetry and mark-recapture studies across European populations report mean dispersal of approximately 4 kilometres, with most events within 10 kilometres of the birth site (Truvé and Lemel 2003; Keuling et al. 2010; Prévot and Licoppe 2013; Morelle et al. 2015). Critically, \(d\) is taken as Dijkstra cost-distance through the resistance surface rather than straight-line distance, so the kernel assigns near-zero risk to cells that are geographically close but separated by a motorway or large water body. The EFSA operational framework gives a validation benchmark (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018): the 3-kilometre protection zone corresponds to a risk of about 0.50 under the kernel with \(D = 4\) km, and the 10-kilometre surveillance boundary to about 0.08, which lets the displayed risk classes be anchored to recognised thresholds.








Figure 2.3: Schematic of the cost-distance infection-risk kernel. Risk decays exponentially from the outbreak origin. Because distance is measured through the resistance surface rather than in a straight line, a barrier casts a low-risk shadow: location B, behind the barrier, carries far lower risk than location A at the same straight-line distance in open terrain. Dashed and dotted circles mark the EFSA protection (about 3 km) and surveillance (about 10 km) thresholds.







2.2.4 Biased Correlated Random Walk
A biased correlated random walk (BCRW) models movement as discrete steps shaped by two forces: directional memory, which correlates successive steps, and an environmental bias toward low-cost terrain (Turchin 1998; Codling et al. 2008). Directional persistence is described by the von Mises distribution, where the probability of a turn \(\theta\) is proportional to \(\exp(\kappa \cos\theta)\) and the concentration \(\kappa\) controls how strongly the walker continues in its current direction. Weighting each candidate step by the inverse of destination resistance and step length adds the cost bias. As the number of walks grows, the BCRW visit density converges toward the circuit-theory current map under the Randomized Shortest Paths equivalence (Saerens et al. 2009), so the two methods estimate the same quantity by different means. In practice this limit is reached only with very many walks, which makes the BCRW a useful complementary diagnostic rather than a replacement for circuit theory.








Figure 2.4: Schematic of a biased correlated random walk. Several stochastic trajectories start from the same source. Directional persistence keeps successive steps roughly aligned, while a bias toward low-cost terrain steers the walks along the low-resistance corridor (green band). Accumulated over many walks, the visit density approximates the circuit-theory current map.







2.2.5 Individual-Based Movement Models
Individual-based movement models take a finer-grained approach by reconstructing movement one step at a time and asking which landscape conditions at the end of each step the animal preferentially selects (Avgar et al. 2016). The integrated step-selection function (iSSF) introduced above is the most widely used method in this class, and the same machinery that calibrates the resistance surface can also drive a forward simulation of individual trajectories. Rather than solving for a global flow as circuit theory does, an iSSF-based individual-based movement model (IBMM) releases simulated agents into the landscape and lets each one move according to the fitted step-length and turning-angle kernels, selecting successive cells in proportion to their estimated habitat suitability. Because the suitability surface is recovered directly from the iSSF coefficients, the simulated paths reflect the same empirically estimated preferences that define the resistance surface, which makes the IBMM a behaviourally explicit complement to the aggregate corridor methods. Its particular value for disease work is that each agent can be given a finite lifespan drawn from an infectious-period distribution, so the accumulated visit pattern estimates how far an infected animal is likely to spread contamination before dying rather than only where movement is possible (Avgar et al. 2016).








Figure 2.5: Schematic of the iSSF-based individual movement model. Infected agents are released from the outbreak origin and move by the fitted step-selection rules. Each agent runs for a finite infectious period drawn from a distribution, so trajectories end (crosses) at different distances. The cells visited before death accumulate into a contamination-probability surface.

title: 2  Theoretical Background
section: 2.3 Wild Boar Ecology Relevant to Connectivity
text:
2.3 Wild Boar Ecology Relevant to Connectivity
The wild boar (Sus scrofa) is a native Eurasian ungulate whose European populations have expanded strongly in recent decades, driven by milder winters, the spread of maize and other high-energy crops, reduced hunting pressure, and supplementary winter feeding (Guberti et al. 2019). Wild boar are habitat generalists that use woodland, especially deciduous and mixed forest, as daytime resting cover and forage at night in agricultural fields, showing marked behavioural flexibility in fragmented and peri-urban landscapes (Morelle et al. 2015). This forest dependence for cover and avoidance of human infrastructure is what a resistance surface must capture. Home ranges are usually well below 50 square kilometres and movement contracts where food is stable and abundant (Guberti et al. 2019; Morelle et al. 2015). The epidemiologically important exception is natal dispersal by young males, which can cover much greater distances and, rarely, exceed 100 kilometres (Guberti et al. 2019), because a dispersing animal in the incubation phase can carry infection into previously unaffected areas.

title: 2  Theoretical Background
section: 2.4 African Swine Fever and the Connectivity Trade-off
text:
2.4 African Swine Fever and the Connectivity Trade-off
ASF is caused by a large DNA virus of the family Asfarviridae that in Europe affects only domestic pigs and wild boar (Guberti et al. 2019). The genotype II strain of the current epidemic has a case fatality rate of 90 to 95 percent, most infected animals die within four to nine days of showing signs, and no licensed vaccine exists, so control depends on surveillance, movement restriction, and population management. The virus is exceptionally stable, remaining infectious in blood for up to 15 weeks and persisting in carcasses for months, so infected carcasses act as long-lived reservoirs that decouple persistence from host density (Guberti et al. 2019). Transmission runs through direct contact, which depends on host density, and through contact with carcasses and fomites, which sustains the cycle even as the live population declines. Since its introduction to the Caucasus in 2007, ASF has advanced westward at roughly 1 to 3 kilometres per month through wild boar populations, with human-induced outbreaks that form new clusters ahead of the front, leaving currently disease-free countries including Switzerland at near-term risk (Guberti et al. 2019).
The more connected and continuous the wild boar population, the faster the epidemic spread advances, while natural or artificial barriers can slow it. This makes connectivity a genuine management variable: authorities can in principle reduce spread by reinforcing barriers, installing targeted fencing in high-connectivity areas, or lowering density in specific corridors. Doing so effectively requires knowing where the corridors and pinch points are and predicting how an intervention would change them. Hess (1994) provided formal support for this and demonstrated that conservation corridors generally aid metapopulation persistence but, under conditions of high direct-contact transmission and high disease-induced mortality that closely match ASF, can substantially raise the risk of disease-driven extinction. The same corridors that benefit red deer can therefore accelerate ASF in wild boar. Existing models, including those of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023), are rigorous but static and cannot answer what-if questions about a proposed fence or overpass. Building a tool that combines their methodological rigour with interactive, user-defined scenarios for wild boar in the Canton of Zürich is the central task of this thesis.

title: 3  Material and Methods
text:
3.1 Software Environment and Data Inputs
The methodology has two phases. The first builds an empirically calibrated wild boar resistance surface from GPS telemetry. The second translates that surface into an interactive QGIS plugin. Full dataset provenance is given in Appendix D and the data sources appendix, and the complete parameter settings of the plugin modules are listed in the statistical appendix, so this chapter keeps to the methodological decisions and their rationale.
The ecological algorithm was developed in R 4.5.1, using terra and sf for spatial handling, amt for movement metrics and step generation, the tidyverse packages for data wrangling, survival for the conditional logistic regression, and car for collinearity diagnostics. The plugin was implemented in Python for QGIS 3.40.13 as Wildboar Connectivity (ASF), version 0.4. Exact package versions are listed in the reproducibility appendix.
Canton Aargau served as the training area where the resistance model was calibrated, and Canton Zürich as the independent transfer area where the plugin was evaluated. A master raster grid was generated for each canton in the Swiss LV95 reference system (EPSG:2056) at 25-metre resolution. To avoid edge effects, each cantonal boundary was buffered by 2,000 metres and converted to a rectangular processing extent, which was then intersected with the national boundary because the high-resolution covariates are restricted to Swiss territory. Extending the study area into Germany was rejected because harmonising Swiss and German topographic and land cover data would have required reconciling incompatible classifications and resolutions, and pan-European products such as CORINE are too coarse to resolve the narrow forest corridors and minor roads that govern wild boar movement at a 15-minute fix interval.
The biological foundation was a GPS telemetry dataset of 36 wild boar tracked in the Aargau study areas of Elfingen and Felsenau between 2014 and 2017 at a 15-minute interval, collected by the Wildlife Management Research Group (WILMA, ZHAW) in the Wildschweinschreck project. This dataset enabled a strictly empirical resistance surface rather than one based on expert opinion. Environmental covariates were derived from swissTLM3D (2026 edition) for forest, roads, railways, settlements, and water, and from the DHM25 elevation model for terrain. Administrative extents came from swissBOUNDARIES3D. Three further datasets supported the transfer to Zürich. The national wildlife passages geodatabase from the FOEN was used to restore permeability at verified crossings. The permanent ASP fence shapefile from the Cantonal Veterinary Office of Zürich was used as an absolute barrier. The WILMA potential core-habitat layer for Zürich was used as a spatial validation anchor and as least-cost-path targets. The role, version, and coordinate system of each dataset are tabulated in the data sources appendix.

title: 3  Material and Methods
text:
3.2 Resistance Surface Pipeline
The pipeline runs in three stages: regularisation and behavioural classification of the telemetry, empirical estimation of habitat preference with an iSSF, and transformation of the coefficients into resistance with the Keeley et al. (2016) exponential function. The design follows the connectivity frameworks of Fischer et al. (2024), Clontz et al. (2021), and Keeley et al. (2016).

3.2.1 Telemetry Processing and Step Classification
All geometries were standardised to LV95. Records with missing or implausible coordinates were removed, timestamps were standardised to UTC, and the first five days of each deployment were dropped as a capture-shock buffer. Deployments with fewer than 100 fixes or spanning under 30 days were excluded, as was one short re-collaring deployment with poor fix quality (the exclusion criteria and the affected deployment are documented in the data sources appendix). Trajectories were resampled to a 15-minute interval with a five-minute tolerance and segmented into temporally continuous bursts, so that step lengths and turning angles were never computed across a data gap. The cleaned dataset yielded 132,388 classified steps.
Because a resistance surface models the cost of travelling between habitat patches rather than behaviour within them, the steps were separated into in-patch and in-matrix (directed transit) states. The fractal and mixture-model approach used for red deer by Fischer et al. (2024) proved unsuitable, because wild boar are highly resident and their transit and resting modes are far less spatially separated than in migratory red deer. A rule-based classifier was therefore developed, applied within each burst, which labels a step as in-matrix if it meets any of three criteria. The first is a step length above 250 metres (Podgórski et al. 2013). The second is a step length above 150 metres combined with a turning angle below \(\pi/4\) in absolute value (Clontz et al. 2021). The third is three or more consecutive steps each above 100 metres with a turning angle below \(\pi/4\) (Benhamou 2014). All other steps were classified as in-patch, and only the in-matrix steps were retained for fitting.


3.2.2 Spatial Covariates
Covariates were derived on the 25-metre master grid using the buffered extent so that focal statistics near the boundary were unbiased. Forest was extracted from swissTLM3D as a binary mask (all-touched rasterisation to preserve narrow tree lines), together with forest density in a 50-metre and a 1000-metre focal window to capture immediate cover and broader landscape context, representing two spatial orders of habitat selection (Johnson 1980), and an unsigned distance-to-forest-edge layer. Slope and the Terrain Ruggedness Index were derived from the DHM25. A combined distance-to-water layer was computed as the cell-wise minimum of distance to flowing water and to standing water, with lakes above one square kilometre held back as absolute barriers. Roads were classified into fenced high-performance roads, main roads, and secondary roads, and combined with railways and settlement polygons. Subsurface segments such as tunnels and underpasses were removed before rasterisation so they do not act as false barriers, and out-of-service and specialty rail lines were dropped. Euclidean distance rasters were computed for each infrastructure class. The exact object-type filters, attribute values, and processing functions are documented in the data sources appendix. Distance to fenced roads was computed but deliberately excluded from the model to avoid a barrier-trapping artifact, described in the variable selection step below.


3.2.3 Integrated Step-Selection Function
The iSSF was fitted on in-matrix steps only, each compared against ten random control steps drawn from the empirical gamma step-length and von Mises turning-angle distributions, which is consistent with established practice (Avgar et al. 2016). Two movement-kernel terms, the log step length and the cosine of the turning angle, were included so that habitat selection is estimated independently of the movement process itself. Covariate values were extracted at each step endpoint, and all continuous covariates were z-standardised using the Aargau training mean and standard deviation, saved as a parameter vector so the same scaling can be reapplied unchanged to Zürich.
A variable selection step removed seven of the fourteen candidate covariates. Slope and the Terrain Ruggedness Index showed extreme mutual collinearity (variance inflation factor above 80) and were non-significant, so both were dropped. Binary forest cover and distance to forest edge were redundant once the two density layers were present. The separate standing and flowing water distances were merged into the combined layer. Distance to fenced roads was excluded because impassable fences force animals to pace along them, producing dense telemetry clusters that a step-selection model misreads as attraction, an artifact addressed instead through the deterministic burn-in. The final model used the clogit function stratified by step, with the seven retained covariates, all of which had variance inflation factors below 1.4.


3.2.4 Resistance Surface Construction and Transfer
The conversion from coefficients to resistance followed the three stages of Keeley et al. (2016). The linear predictor was formed for every cell as the weighted sum of the scaled covariates,
\[\eta = \sum_k \hat{\beta}_k \cdot x_{k,\text{scaled}},\]
normalised to a suitability surface \(S \in [0,1]\) by min-max scaling, and transformed to resistance by
\[R = \exp\!\left(C \cdot (1 - S)\right), \qquad C = 4,\]
as used by Fischer et al. (2024), giving a theoretical range of 1 for the most preferred habitat to about 54.6 for the least. A deterministic burn-in then assigned absolute values in a fixed order, because later assignments overwrite earlier ones where masks overlap: small water bodies received a high finite cost, all infrastructure cells received the maximum resistance, fenced motorways and large lakes were set to NoData as absolute barriers, and finally wildlife passages were set to the minimum resistance so that verified crossings remain fully permeable.
The Zürich surface was built by recomputing identical covariates for the Zürich extent and applying the Aargau coefficients and scaling parameters without re-estimation. The only change was that the final normalisation used the Zürich linear-predictor range rather than the Aargau range, so that the full suitability scale is used for within-Zürich differentiation. This choice maximises corridor contrast within Zürich at the cost of making absolute resistance values non-comparable between cantons, which is acceptable because the analysis is confined to Zürich. The burn-in was applied identically, with the permanent ASP fences added as absolute barriers before the wildlife-passage step.

title: 3  Material and Methods
text:
3.3 QGIS Plugin Development
The second phase translated the validated resistance surface into an interactive decision-support tool. The Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) plugin lets a wildlife or veterinary user load the pre-computed resistance raster, define a hypothetical outbreak location with a map click, draw virtual fences or place wildlife overpasses on the canvas, and immediately recompute connectivity to compare scenarios. All computation runs in a background thread so the interface stays responsive.

3.3.1 Architecture and Interaction Model
The plugin is organised as cooperating Python modules with bounded responsibilities: an entry-point module that registers the plugin and owns the dialog and map tools, two custom map tools for point selection and polyline drawing, a stateless resistance-editor that returns a modified copy of the array without ever writing to the source raster, a background task that implements the five analyses, and a subprocess wrapper for the Circuitscape.jl solver. Communication between user actions and logic uses the Qt signal-and-slot mechanism, so the drawing tools carry out no computation themselves. The dialog exposes a resistance-raster selector, an optional habitat-polygon selector for least-cost-path targets, the three drawing tools, and five checkboxes selecting which analyses to run.


3.3.2 Landscape Modification
When the user runs an analysis, accumulated fences and overpasses are transformed into the raster coordinate system and applied to a deep copy of the loaded resistance window, so the source file is never altered. Fence polylines are rasterised with all-touched coverage and dilated to a two-cell-wide ribbon of NaN, making them indistinguishable from the absolute barriers already encoded in the surface. Overpasses are stamped as small discs of minimum resistance, and this overwrite is bidirectional, so an overpass placed on a motorway replaces the NaN with a passable value, correctly representing a crossing punched through an otherwise impassable structure.


3.3.3 Analysis Window, Source, and Cost Grid
The analysis is restricted to a window centred on the outbreak origin, extending 10,000 metres plus a 1,500-metre edge buffer in each direction and snapped to the integer pixel grid of the source so that outputs are not shifted relative to the input. The outbreak source is a disc of finite-resistance cells around the origin, snapped to the nearest passable cell if the click lands on a barrier. A single Dijkstra sweep from the source disc, using an 8-connected geometric cost metric that penalises diagonal moves, produces a cost grid giving every reachable cell its minimum cumulative cost, while cells behind absolute barriers receive infinite cost and define the boundary of the reachable area of interest.


3.3.4 The Five Analyses
The least-cost path module connects the origin to the nearest reachable habitat clusters, taken either from a user-supplied habitat layer or auto-detected by thresholding the resistance raster, and traces each route back through the Dijkstra grid. Shared segments accumulate strength so that the backbone corridor serving many or large clusters is highlighted, and the network is styled in graduated blue.
The infection-risk module converts the cost grid into a continuous probability surface, \(\text{risk}(d) = \exp(-d/D_{\text{cost}})\), where \(D_{\text{cost}}\) rescales the published 4-kilometre mean wild boar dispersal distance into cost units using the pixel size and the median resistance of the window. The result is classified into three EFSA-aligned zones, with the high-risk class anchored to the 3-kilometre protection zone and the medium class to the 10-kilometre surveillance zone (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018).
The pinchpoint module treats the window as a resistor network and injects current from the source to the boundary, identifying where movement concentrates. The preferred solver is Circuitscape.jl, called as a Julia subprocess, with a pure-Python scipy sparse Laplacian solver as a fallback that produces equivalent results more slowly.
The biased correlated random walk releases many walkers from the source disc, each selecting steps by the product of a cost weight and a von Mises directional-persistence weight, and accumulates a visit-density surface that provides an independent stochastic check on the pinchpoint result, toward which it converges at large walk numbers (Saerens et al. 2009).
The iSSF-based individual movement model simulates infected animals from the origin, each running for a stochastically drawn infectious period and selecting steps by habitat suitability recovered by inverting the Keeley transformation, \(S = 1 - \ln R / C\). The fraction of animals visiting each cell gives a contamination-probability surface that quantifies disease reach rather than movement capacity alone. The infectious-period distribution and the movement-kernel parameters of these modules are calibrated to EFSA virological data and to ASF studies in European wild boar (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018; Probst et al. 2017; Chenais et al. 2019), and the full numerical settings are listed in the statistical appendix.

title: 4  Results
text:
4.1 Resistance Surface
Two primary deliverables emerged from this project: a 25-metre resolution wild boar resistance surface covering Canton Aargau (used for model calibration) and Canton Zürich (produced by parameter transfer), and the Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) QGIS plugin that uses this resistance surface as its analytical input. The following sections present the results in the order of their production: from telemetry data quality and step classification through spatial covariate construction, iSSF model fitting, and resistance surface generation, concluding with a functional demonstration of the interactive plugin.
In the following section the results of creating the resistance surface are shown and explained in detail.

title: 4  Results
text:
4.1.1 Telemetry Quality and Step Classification
GPS telemetry from 36 wild boar individuals tracked in Canton Aargau between 2014 and 2017 was resampled to a consistent 15-minute fix interval before step extraction. One short re-collaring deployment (027_Agat_13970) was excluded from analysis because it retained only 50.6% of on-schedule fixes alongside a high proportion of duplicate fixes at one-minute intervals, indicating a recording malfunction rather than genuine movement data. The remaining deployments retained at least 90% of unique scheduled fixes after the duplicate-collapse step. After applying the minimum-fix and minimum-duration thresholds, 13 individuals were retained for step extraction, and the cleaned dataset yielded a total of 132,388 classified steps.
The three-rule hierarchical classifier partitioned these steps into 7,810 in-matrix transit steps and 124,578 in-patch resting steps. Among in-matrix steps, Rule 1 (step length greater than 250 metres) captured 4,752 steps (60.8% of all in-matrix steps), Rule 2 (step length greater than 150 metres and absolute turning angle below π/4 radians) contributed 2,741 steps (35.1%), and Rule 3 (three or more consecutive directional steps each exceeding 100 metres) added 317 steps (4.1%). The in-matrix dataset served as the sole analytical sample for iSSF fitting. In-patch steps were excluded from the model because they describe resting and foraging behaviour within habitat patches rather than landscape-level transit between patches, and combining the two behavioural states would confound the resistance surface.
In-matrix step lengths ranged from 100 metres to 5,424 metres with a mean of 299 metres, a median of 273 metres, and a standard deviation of 163 metres. The distribution is right-skewed, consistent with the gamma-distributed step-length kernel assumed by the iSSF movement model. Turning angles were approximately symmetric around zero with a standard deviation of approximately 59 degrees, indicating moderate directional persistence during transit. Which shows that the step classification worked.

4.1.2 iSSF Model Coefficients and Variable Selection
Before fitting the final conditional logistic regression, seven covariates were removed from the original set of 14 based on a VIF (variance inflation factor) test. Slope and terrain ruggedness index (TRI) had VIF values exceeding 80, driven by their near-collinearity. Binary forest cover and Distance to forest Edge were removed because they were insignificant when the forest density layers were added. Distance to flowing water and distance to lakes were merged into a single combined distance-to-water layer before covariate assembly, and the two original layers were then removed. Distance to fenced road was excluded because its extreme landscape sparsity in Aargau (fenced motorway infrastructure is confined to a small number of access and exit segments within the study area) produced a spatial trapping pattern: in-matrix steps were concentrated near the few fenced road segments present, inflating the coefficient and making it non-transferable to other landscapes. The seven remaining covariates formed the final iSSF model.
All seven selection coefficients were positive and statistically significant at the α = 0.05 level, indicating that wild boar in the in-matrix transit state preferentially selected landscape cells offering higher forest density, stronger forest density gradients, and greater distance from all infrastructure categories and from water. The two strongest selection effects were of nearly equal magnitude: forest density at the 50-metre scale (β = 0.516, z = 29.14) and distance to railway (β = 0.505, z = 4.40). The former reflects the central role of dense forest as movement habitat, while the latter reflects the strong avoidance of railway infrastructure during transit. Forest density gradient at the 1,000-metre scale was the third-ranked predictor (β = 0.253), capturing preference for cells situated within a landscape matrix of increasing forest cover rather than in isolated patches. Distance to main road (β = 0.244), distance to settlement (β = 0.210), and distance to secondary road (β = 0.171) followed, all expressing avoidance of the built and road environment. Distance to water was the weakest but still significant predictor (β = 0.059, p = 0.012), consistent with wild boar avoiding stream crossings during directed transit movement.

4.1.3 Intermediate Spatial Covariate Layers
Fourteen spatial covariates were assembled on the 25-metre Aargau grid before VIF testing. These are presented below in functional groups. Layers included in the final iSSF model are labelled accordingly. Excluded layers are shown to document the full intermediate output of the pipeline and to provide spatial context for understanding the final resistance surface structure. For all distance rasters, values are in metres measured as Euclidean distance to the nearest cell of the target feature class. For all density and suitability rasters, values range from 0 to 1. Binary barrier and passage rasters contain value 1 where the feature is present and are stored as NoData elsewhere.

4.1.3.1 Forest Covariates
The forest cover layer classified 41.0% of valid cells as forest, reflecting the mosaic of wooded slopes and agricultural lowlands characteristic of the Aargau study area. Forest density at the 50-metre scale is a continuous proportion expressing local canopy cover intensity, and at a mean of 0.41 it closely mirrors the binary cover fraction. The 1,000-metre forest density gradient captures the same quantity smoothed over a broader landscape window, producing a spatially coarser surface that records the transition from the forested Jura foothills to the open Mittelland plain. Both density layers were included in the final iSSF model. The binary forest cover and the forest-edge distance layer were excluded during VIF testing.








Figure 4.3: Forest-related covariate layers for the Aargau study area at aggregated display resolution (125 m). Left: Binary forest cover (0 = non-forest, 1 = forest). Centre: Forest density at the 50-metre scale (proportion of forest cells within a 50-m moving window). Right: Forest density at the 1,000-metre scale (gradient proxy). The 50-metre and 1,000-metre density layers were included in the final iSSF model. Binary forest cover and forest-edge distance (not shown) were excluded by VIF testing.





The distance-to-forest-edge layer, excluded for redundancy with the two forest density layers, is mapped in the appendix (Figure B.1).


4.1.3.2 Terrain Covariates
Slope and terrain ruggedness index were computed from the DHM25 digital elevation model at 25-metre resolution. Slope in the study area ranged from 0 to 69 degrees with a mean of 8.1 degrees, reflecting the gentle topography of the Aargau lowlands with steeper values confined to the Jura slopes. TRI ranged from 0 to 54.5 with a mean of 2.9, indicating overall low topographic roughness. Both layers were excluded from the final iSSF model because of extreme collinearity (VIF exceeding 80 in both cases).
Both terrain layers (slope and TRI) are mapped in the appendix (Figure B.2).


4.1.3.3 Water Covariates
Distance to water was the final covariate used in the iSSF model. It was derived by merging the distance-to-flowing-water and distance-to-lake layers into a single combined distance-to-any-water surface by taking the cell-wise minimum of the two component rasters. Distance to flowing water alone ranged from 0 to 3,466 metres (mean 242 m), reflecting the dense stream network of the Aargau lowlands. Distance to lakes was considerably larger on average (mean 978 m, maximum 7,164 m) because standing water bodies are spatially sparse in the study area. The combined distance-to-water surface (mean 225 m) therefore largely reflects proximity to streams. The component layers were excluded after merging to avoid double-counting the water feature class in the VIF testing.








Figure 4.4: Water proximity covariates. Left: Distance to flowing water (m). Centre: Distance to lakes (m). Right: Combined distance to any water body (m), used in the final iSSF model. The combined layer was derived as the cell-wise minimum of the two component layers.







4.1.3.4 Infrastructure Distance Covariates
The four infrastructure distance layers that entered the final iSSF model show strongly different spatial structures reflecting the hierarchy of the transport network. Distance to main road ranged from 0 to 7,092 metres with a mean of 747 metres, documenting that the Aargau study area is relatively well served by the cantonal and national road network. Distance to secondary road had a much lower mean of 160 metres and a maximum of only 3,250 metres, indicating that secondary roads permeate the agricultural lowlands at close intervals. Distance to railway had the largest mean (1,756 metres) and range (0 to 7,243 metres) of all infrastructure covariates, reflecting the coarser spacing of the rail network compared with roads. Distance to settlement ranged from 0 to 6,976 metres (mean 206 metres), with low values concentrated in the densely settled Aare valley floor.








Figure 4.5: Infrastructure distance covariates included in the final iSSF model. All distances are in metres. Higher values (darker blue) indicate greater separation from the respective infrastructure class, which the positive iSSF coefficients show to be strongly preferred by wild boar during transit.





The distance-to-fenced-road layer, while part of the initial covariate set, was excluded from the iSSF model before VIF testing because of a recognised trapping artifact. Fenced motorway infrastructure in Aargau is spatially sparse (mean distance 4,179 metres, maximum 16,710 metres), and the few in-matrix GPS steps recorded near fenced segments were disproportionately concentrated there relative to the available landscape. This creates a positive correlation between fenced-road proximity and step selection that reflects the limited geographic extent of the feature rather than genuine habitat preference, and the coefficient was not considered transferable to Zürich where fenced motorway density is substantially higher.
The distance-to-fenced-road layer is mapped in the appendix (Figure B.3).


4.1.3.5 Absolute Barrier and Wildlife Passage Layers
Four binary layers defined the cells that received NoData (impassable) or minimum resistance (passable) treatment in the Keeley burn-in step, independently of the iSSF. Highway cells (motorways, motorway approaches, exit ramps, and car-train carriers) and cells within large water bodies exceeding 1 km² in area were set to NoData. Cells within large settlement polygons (defined as the union of named settlement areas exceeding a size threshold) were also set to NoData. Wildlife passage locations were set to the minimum resistance value R = 1, ensuring that validated crossing structures function as zero-cost corridors in the connectivity model. Together these four layers account for the 10.8% of cells coded as NoData in the final Aargau resistance raster.

The Aargau resistance raster covers 2,224 × 2,405 pixels at 25-metre resolution in the Swiss LV95 coordinate system (EPSG:2056), with a 2-kilometre buffer applied around the cantonal boundary to avoid edge effects in subsequent analyses. Resistance values span the full theoretical range of the Keeley transformation: from 1.00 (maximum suitability, minimum resistance) to 54.60, which equals exp(4) within numerical precision and corresponds to cells with effectively zero iSSF selection weight. The median resistance of 34.25 lies well above the midpoint of the valid range (approximately 27.8), indicating that the study area is predominantly high-resistance terrain from the perspective of a dispersing wild boar. The 75th and 90th percentiles of resistance are 44.54 and 54.60 respectively, and at least 10% of valid cells sit at the theoretical maximum.
Spatially, low-resistance cells (R below 10, corresponding to suitability above 0.43) are concentrated in the large continuous forest blocks on the south-facing Jura slopes and in the riparian forests along the Aare and Reuss rivers. These areas provide the dense, well-structured forest with low infrastructure proximity that the iSSF identified as the dominant selection signal. High-resistance cells (R approaching 54.60) dominate the agricultural plain and all areas within short distances of the road, rail, and settlement infrastructure network that dissects the Mittelland. title: 4  Results
text:
4.2 QGIS Plugin
The Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) plugin was implemented as a QGIS 3.40 extension and tested against the Zürich resistance raster with the WILMA core habitat polygons as LCP destination targets. Functional testing confirmed that all five analytical modules produced spatially coherent outputs for a range of outbreak origin locations across the canton. Two scenarios are reported here: a baseline analysis at an unmodified outbreak location in a forested area, and a scenario comparison demonstrating the effect of drawing a virtual fence across a corridor identified by the pinchpoint analysis.

4.2.1 Baseline Connectivity Analysis
For the baseline demonstration, the outbreak origin was placed in a forested grid cell north of the Zürich city centre representative of a scenario in which the disease enters through a wild boar population dispersing along the Zürichsee hills. All five outputs were enabled, with 500 BCRW realisations and 2,000 iSSF-IBMM agents. The analysis completed in under three minutes on a standard laptop.
The LCP corridor analysis connected the outbreak origin to the nearest reachable WILMA habitat clusters via the pre-computed Dijkstra cost grid. The graduated blue styling assigned light sky blue to spur corridors serving single small clusters, vivid blue to intermediate connectors, and deep navy to the backbone segments shared by multiple routes. The backbone concentrated in the forested ridgelines between valley systems, consistent with the visual pattern of low-resistance cells in the Zürich resistance map.
The circuit-theory pinchpoint raster, computed using Circuitscape.jl via Julia subprocess, showed concentrated current density at several forested ridge crossings and at the narrowest sections of the wooded corridors linking habitat clusters separated by the motorway and rail network. These pinchpoints represent the locations where a fence intervention would produce the largest reduction in connectivity at lowest material cost.
The continuous infection-risk raster produced three discrete EFSA-aligned zones around the origin. The high-risk zone (risk above 0.50) extended approximately 2.5 to 3.5 kilometres in the least-resistant directions, consistent with its calibration to the 4-kilometre mean wild boar dispersal distance. The EFSA surveillance zone boundary (risk 0.15) was reached at cost-equivalent distances of approximately 7 to 8 kilometres through continuous forest and at shorter Euclidean distances across fragmented terrain.
The BCRW density and iSSF-IBMM contamination probability layers broadly corroborated the LCP and pinchpoint structure. The BCRW density surface showed the highest visitation counts along the same ridgeline corridors identified by the LCP analysis, confirming their role as preferred transit routes. The iSSF-IBMM log10-transformed contamination probability surface showed the steepest probability gradients at the forest-to-open-land transitions where resistance increases rapidly.

4.2.2 Scenario Comparison: Virtual Fence Intervention
To demonstrate the scenario comparison functionality, a virtual fence was drawn along a motorway access road that crosses one of the principal pinchpoints identified in the baseline analysis. The fence was rasterized as a two-cell-wide NaN wall in the modified resistance array and the full analysis was rerun without changing the outbreak origin or any other parameter. Both runs used identical settings so that all differences in the output layers can be attributed entirely to the fence modification.
The pinchpoint raster showed a clear rerouting of current density away from the blocked corridor segment. The cumulative flow that previously concentrated at the motorway crossing was redistributed to the two nearest alternative corridors, which showed increased current density in the post-fence scenario. The LCP backbone similarly shifted away from the blocked crossing, with the backbone corridor segments immediately upstream and downstream of the fence position being replaced by longer, more costly alternative routes. The infection-risk zone contracted asymmetrically on the side of the fence facing away from the outbreak origin, indicating reduced modelled reachability in the fenced direction.

Left: Baseline pinchpoint current density. Right: Post-fence pinchpoint current density. The fence segment (red line) blocks the principal corridor crossing, forcing redistributed current density toward secondary corridors visible as increased brightness in the right panel. Replace both panels with screenshots captured from QGIS after completing the baseline and fence-modification runs.





The scenario comparison illustrates the core purpose of the plugin: rather than producing a single static map, it enables iterative exploration of management alternatives within the same GIS session. A wildlife manager can test different fence alignments, observe how each one redirects the modelled corridor network, and compare the resulting infection-risk zones, all without leaving the QGIS environment or re-running any preprocessing steps.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.1 Ecological Interpretation of the iSSF Model
This thesis set out to adapt a connectivity modeling framework for wild boar by building an empirically calibrated resistance surface, to develop an interactive QGIS plugin for testing landscape modifications, and to produce scenario-contrast visualisations for wildlife authorities in Canton Zürich. The following sections evaluate how far each objective was reached, place the findings in context, and set out the principal uncertainties.
All seven retained covariates were positive predictors of transit movement, confirming that wild boar in directed movement prefer denser forest at both scales and greater distance from every class of transport and settlement infrastructure. This matches the established ecology of the species, which depends on continuous forest cover for movement and strongly avoids traffic, light, and disturbance (Morelle et al. 2015; Guberti et al. 2019). Two features of the coefficient structure stand out. Forest density at the 50-metre scale carried by far the smallest standard error, reflecting the central role of immediate cover. Distance to railway carried a nearly identical point estimate but with a much larger standard error, most likely because railways are sparse in the Aargau training area and few transit steps were recorded near them, so the avoidance effect is real but its magnitude is less certain. The positive coefficients at both forest scales indicate selection for cells that are both locally wooded and embedded in a forested matrix, consistent with hierarchical habitat selection (Avgar et al. 2016). The non-significance of slope and terrain ruggedness reflects the modest relief of the lowland training area and should not be generalised, since terrain may well enter a model calibrated in more rugged landscapes.
The exclusion of distance to fenced roads is a transferable methodological point. Including it produced an ecologically implausible apparent attraction toward motorway fencing, an artifact of animals pacing along impassable barriers and generating dense telemetry clusters. Handling such hard barriers through the deterministic burn-in rather than as a step-selection covariate is the correct response, and any iSSF study in a landscape with dense linear barriers should apply the same check before finalising variable selection.

title: 5  Discussion
section: 5.2 Resistance Surface Quality and Transfer Validity
text:
5.2 Resistance Surface Quality and Transfer Validity
The Aargau surface reproduces the expected corridor structure, with low resistance along the forested Jura slopes and the Aare and Reuss riparian forests and high resistance across the agricultural plain and peri-urban areas. The median resistance well above the scale midpoint confirms that the lowland landscape is predominantly unfavourable for transit, consistent with its known fragmentation (Fischer et al. 2024). Assigning dense settlement the maximum resistance rather than NoData is a deliberate compromise: wild boar do enter urban fringes nocturnally (Guberti et al. 2019; Morelle et al. 2015), so treating settlement as an absolute barrier would suppress pathways that occur in reality, and pathways routed through such cells should be read as rare but possible.
Transferring the Aargau parameters to Zürich is operationally necessary because no Zürich telemetry was available, and it rests on the assumption that wild boar respond to forest and infrastructure similarly in both cantons. This is plausible given their shared Mittelland structure and the broadly consistent habitat preferences of European wild boar (Morelle et al. 2015), but the more intensively urbanised Greater Zürich landscape may host animals with modified avoidance responses that the Aargau coefficients do not capture. Reusing the Aargau scaling parameters is what keeps the coefficients interpretable, while the Zürich-specific final normalisation maximises corridor contrast within Zürich at the cost of cross-cantonal comparability, an acceptable trade-off for a Zürich-only analysis. No permanent ASP fences fell within the Zürich extent at the time of data delivery, so the surface is currently unaffected by fence infrastructure, though the pipeline is ready to incorporate new installations.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.3 The Planning Tool in Context
The central advance over the static models of Fischer et al. (2024) and Urbina et al. (2023) is interactivity. Both provide rigorous maps of the current landscape but cannot answer the what-if questions that ASF management requires. The plugin closes this gap: a user can draw a fence across a pinchpoint, re-run the model, and see directly how the corridor backbone, the infection-risk zones, and the contamination surface respond. This addresses the trade-off Hess (1994) identified, where the same corridor that benefits a species can accelerate disease, by showing both sides of a specific intervention rather than a general map.
The five modules are complementary rather than redundant. Least-cost paths give the optimal routes, circuit theory reveals bottlenecks and redundancy that a single path cannot (McRae et al. 2008), the infection-risk raster expresses cost-distance as an EFSA-anchored probability that veterinary authorities can read directly, the biased correlated random walk offers an independent stochastic check that converges toward the circuit result (Saerens et al. 2009), and the individual-based model adds an epidemiological layer by simulating disease trajectories conditioned on an ASF infectious period. Using the published Circuitscape.jl solver, with settings matching Urbina et al. (2023), favours a validated implementation over a custom one, while the scipy fallback preserves the capability where Julia is unavailable.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.4 Limitations and Sources of Uncertainty
The most significant limitation is the absence of formal validation. The iSSF fit was not quantified with concordance statistics or spatial cross-validation, and predictive performance on held-out Aargau steps was not assessed, so the relationship between modeled resistance and actual movement probability remains uncertain (Avgar et al. 2016). The Zürich surface is entirely unvalidated, since no Zürich tracks were available to test the transferred corridors, which adds a layer of uncertainty to management decisions based on the Zürich map. A gap of roughly ten years separates the 2014 to 2017 telemetry from the 2026 landscape data, so infrastructure and land cover changes are not reflected in the behavioural calibration, and their net effect was not assessed. The 15-minute fix interval reliably captures directed transit (Podgórski et al. 2013; Benhamou 2014) but the conservative classifier may exclude some shorter in-matrix steps, slightly underestimating selection strength, though the large retained sample and high significance of all predictors suggest the coefficients are robust. Finally, the plugin modules carry their own assumptions: the infectious-period distribution is calibrated to Eastern European and Baltic populations (European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2018; Probst et al. 2017; Chenais et al. 2019) whose disease course may differ from ASF-naive Swiss wild boar, and the static movement kernel does not capture nocturnal or seasonal variation in space use.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.5 Practical Implications and Outlook
The tool is primarily a pre-outbreak planning instrument. Its main value is enabling authorities to identify high-risk corridors and prioritise fence locations before an incursion, with the pinchpoint map showing where a small barrier achieves the greatest reduction in connectivity and the infection-risk raster showing which zones would require surveillance under EFSA guidelines. The scenario comparison supports the iterative decision-making that operational management needs, letting an officer test alternative fence alignments in a single session without programming or reprocessing.
The pipeline follows the FAIR principles of the ZHAW reproducibility requirement, drawing on publicly accessible federal geodata except for the partner-provided telemetry and fence data, with the full workflow encoded in documented notebooks and the plugin distributed as an installable QGIS package reusable in other cantons. Three extensions would add the most value. The highest priority is obtaining GPS telemetry from Zürich wild boar to validate the transferred surface against independent movement data. A seasonal decomposition of the iSSF would reflect the substantial behavioural shifts between winter mast foraging and the active season (Morelle et al. 2015). Finally, weighting the outputs by estimated wild boar density would add the host-abundance dimension that, together with connectivity, drives epidemic spread (Guberti et al. 2019).

section: A.2 Telemetry Data Quality and Exclusions
text:
A.2 Telemetry Data Quality and Exclusions
The raw telemetry comprised 36 GSM-GPS deployments recorded at a nominal 15-minute fix interval. The following cleaning and exclusion steps were applied before any movement statistics were computed. The first five days of each deployment were removed as a capture-shock buffer. Deployments with fewer than 100 fixes or spanning less than 30 days after cleaning were excluded. One deployment, 027_Agat_13970, was removed because it was a short re-collaring of an animal already represented by a longer deployment (027_Agat_13969) and retained only 50.6 percent of its scheduled fixes. After duplicate collapse, the remaining deployments retained at least 90 percent of unique scheduled fixes, yielding 132,388 classified steps of which 7,810 were in-matrix transit steps.

title: Appendix A — Data Sources and Input Datasets
text:
A.3 Detailed Layer Processing
This section records the dataset-specific processing decisions that were condensed in the methods chapter, so that the pipeline remains fully reproducible.
swissBOUNDARIES3D (version 1.5, swisstopo). Administrative geometries were extracted from the TLM_KANTONSGEBIET polygon feature class. The dataset has a stated geometric accuracy of about ±0.5 metres in position and elevation. Extracted cantonal geometries were buffered by 2,000 metres and converted to a rectangular processing extent, passed as a Well-Known Text filter to the vector reading functions to load only intersecting geometries.
swissTLM3D (2026 edition, swisstopo). Forest was taken from the tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung layer, retaining closed forest (“Wald”), open forest (“Wald offen”), scrub (“Gebueschwald”), and woody areas (“Gehoelzflaeche”), and excluding unstocked forest, mining areas, orchards, cemeteries, vineyards, and water-body areas. Roads from tlm_strassen_strasse were classified into fenced high-performance roads (“Autobahn”, “Autostrasse”, “Ausfahrt”, “Einfahrt”, “Zufahrt”, “Autozug”), main roads (“10m/8m/6m Strasse”), and secondary roads (“4m/3m Strasse”, “2m Weg”, “Verbindung”, “Dienstzufahrt”, “Platz”). Settlements used the tlm_namen_siedlungsname polygon classes “Ort”, “Ortsteil”, “Quartier”, and “Quartierteil”, preferred over building footprints because wild boar respond to the contiguous built-up matrix. All linear features were reduced to two dimensions on import. A prep_above_ground() function removed subsurface segments using the STUFE vertical-position attribute (retaining values of zero or greater) and the KUNSTBAUTE attribute (removing “Tunnel”, “Unterfuehrung”, “Unterführung”, “in Gebaeude”, “in Gebäude”, in both ASCII and Unicode spellings). A clean_railways() function removed out-of-service lines and funiculars, rack railways, and heritage lines. Binary presence rasters used all-touched rasterisation, and Euclidean distance rasters were computed for each class.
Forest structure. A binary forest mask, a 50-metre and a 1000-metre circular focal-density layer, and an unsigned distance-to-forest-edge layer were derived from the forest mask. The two density layers represent the immediate (micro-canopy) and macro-scale orders of habitat selection.
Water. Standing water from tlm_gewaesser_stehendes_gewaesser was reconstructed from three-dimensional shoreline multi-line strings into polygons (Z dropped, grouped by gwl_nr, unioned, line-merged, cast to polygons), with island polygons subtracted. Lakes above one square kilometre were held as absolute barriers. Flowing water from tlm_gewaesser_fliessgewaesser retained only surface-level features (verlauf of “Oberirdisch”, “Bruecke”, or “Wasserfall”), excluding piped and subterranean streams. A combined distance-to-water layer was computed as the cell-wise minimum of the two components.
DHM25 (swisstopo). Slope and the Terrain Ruggedness Index were derived at the native 25-metre resolution. The DHM25 is referenced to LV03 (EPSG:21781), assigned manually before processing, and was reprojected to LV95 by bilinear interpolation. Its vertical accuracy is about ±1.5 metres on the Swiss Plateau and ±3 to ±8 metres in Alpine terrain, and its altitude data were surveyed between 1952 and 1979 with final updates in 1999, so recent terrain alterations are not represented.
Wildlife passages (FOEN, N2023). The N2023_Version_Wildtierpassagen polygons were reprojected to LV95, buffered by 30 metres, and rasterised so that verified crossings override the barrier effect of fenced motorways.
Permanent ASP fences (Cantonal Veterinary Office Zürich). The Dauerzaeune.shp woven-wire fences were rasterised and burned in as absolute barriers in the Zürich surface only.
WILMA core habitats (December 2024). The Potenzial_Wildschwein_Kerneinstaende_ZH_2024_WILMA.shp layer delineates predictive potential resting habitats and was used as a spatial validation anchor and as least-cost-path targets, not as confirmed animal presence.

B.1 Final iSSF Coefficients
This appendix collects the full statistical output of the integrated step-selection function and the parameter settings of the five plugin analysis modules, so that the results in the main text can be reproduced and audited.
The final conditional logistic regression was fitted on 7,810 in-matrix transit steps from 36 GPS-collared individuals in Canton Aargau, each compared against ten random control steps. All covariates are z-standardised with the Aargau training mean and standard deviation. The seven retained coefficients, ordered by magnitude, are reproduced in Table 4.2 in the results chapter and summarised here for reference: forest density at the 50-metre scale (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.513\)), distance to railway (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.513\)), forest density gradient at the 1000-metre scale (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.245\)), distance to settlement (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.224\)), distance to main road (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.218\)), distance to secondary road (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.149\)), and distance to water (\(\hat{\beta} = 0.051\)). All coefficients were positive and significant at the 0.05 level, and all variance inflation factors for the retained set were below 1.4.

title: Appendix B — Statistical Outputs and Model Parameters
text:
B.3 Plugin Analysis Parameters
The five analytical modules of the Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) plugin use the following fixed parameters. The analysis window extends 11,500 metres in each direction from the outbreak origin (a 10,000-metre buffer plus a 1,500-metre edge buffer). The infection-risk kernel uses the published mean natal dispersal distance of European wild boar of 4 kilometres, with the EFSA protection zone (3 km) and surveillance zone (10 km) mapped to risk thresholds of 0.50 and 0.15. The biased correlated random walk uses a von Mises concentration of \(\kappa = 2.0\), a 2,000-step limit, and 500 realisations by default. The iSSF-based individual movement model runs 2,000 agents by default, draws the infectious period from a \(\text{Gamma}(\alpha = 3, \beta = 3.5\,\text{days})\) distribution (mean 10.5 days), and generates 25 candidate steps per move using a gamma step-length kernel (shape 2.653, scale 160 m) and a von Mises turning kernel (\(\kappa = 1.064\)).

B.5 Excluded Covariate Layers
The following maps document the covariate layers that were computed in the pipeline but excluded from the final iSSF model. They are provided here for completeness and spatial context.








Figure B.1: Distance to forest edge (metres) for the Aargau study area. Values range from 25 m (the minimum possible at 25-metre resolution) to 3,281 m. This layer was excluded from the final iSSF model because of its high VIF with the forest density layers.













Figure B.2: Terrain covariates derived from the DHM25 digital elevation model. Left: Slope in degrees. Right: Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI, dimensionless). Both layers were excluded from the final iSSF model due to extreme multicollinearity with the forest density layers (VIF > 80).













Figure B.3: Distance to fenced road (motorway and motorway access segments) in the Aargau study area. The extreme spatial sparsity of this feature (mean 4,179 m, maximum 16,710 m) produced a barrier-trapping artifact in the iSSF and led to exclusion of this covariate before model fitting.

title: Appendix D — Statement of Reproducibility
text:
D.1 Code and Workflow
This thesis follows the FAIR principles for data and code management specified in the ZHAW Statement of Reproducibility.
The complete analytical workflow is encoded in two Quarto notebooks. The resistance surface pipeline, from raw telemetry to the final 25-metre resistance raster, is contained in scripts/01_create_resistance_surface.ipynb. All connectivity analyses are contained in scripts/02_connectivity.ipynb. Given the same input data and software environment, both notebooks produce identical outputs deterministically. The QGIS plugin Wildboar Connectivity (ASF) is distributed as a standard QGIS Python package with a metadata.txt manifest and can be installed through the QGIS plugin manager.
